lesson.title: How Much Charge Fits? Quantifying a Capacitor's Capacity
lesson.summary: Capacitance measures how much charge a capacitor stores per volt applied, and it is set entirely by the plate area, plate separation, and insulating material used.
lesson.body:
Capacitance is the number that tells you how much charge a capacitor can store for each volt applied across it. Formally, capacitance is defined as C equals Q divided by V, where Q is the charge in coulombs and V is the voltage in volts. The unit is the farad, named for Michael Faraday, and one farad means one coulomb of charge is stored for every one volt applied. A farad turns out to be an enormous amount of capacitance for a real component to hold in a small package, so almost every capacitor you will handle is rated in microfarads, one millionth of a farad, nanofarads, one billionth, or picofarads, one trillionth, with only specialized supercapacitors reaching into the farad range themselves.

What actually sets a capacitor's capacitance value is its physical construction. For the simplest case, two flat parallel plates facing each other, the formula is C equals epsilon times A divided by d, where A is the area of overlap between the plates, d is the distance separating them, and epsilon is the permittivity of whatever insulating material fills that gap. Permittivity is usually written as epsilon-zero, the permittivity of empty space, multiplied by epsilon-r, a relative factor describing how much better the filling material supports an electric field than a vacuum does. Epsilon-zero has a fixed, measured value of 8.854 times 10 to the negative twelfth farads per meter. The next chapter looks closely at how the choice of insulating material, the dielectric, changes epsilon-r and therefore the whole capacitance.

Put numbers to it. Imagine two flat plates, each with an overlapping area of 100 square centimeters, which is 0.01 square meters, separated by an air gap 1 millimeter thick, or 0.001 meters, with air treated as essentially the same as vacuum so epsilon-r is approximately 1. The capacitance is C equals epsilon-zero times A divided by d, so C equals 8.854 times 10 to the negative twelfth, times 0.01, divided by 0.001. Multiplying the top gives 8.854 times 10 to the negative fourteenth, and dividing by 0.001 shifts the exponent by three, giving 8.854 times 10 to the negative eleventh farads, which is 88.54 picofarads. That is a genuinely small capacitance, which is exactly why real capacitors rarely look like two flat plates in open air.

To reach the microfarad values common in real circuits, manufacturers cannot simply build larger and larger flat plates, since that would make components impossibly bulky. Instead they roll long strips of foil and thin insulating film into a tight cylinder, or stack many layers of metal and ceramic on top of each other, packing enormous effective plate area into a small volume. Some designs also use a dielectric material with a much higher epsilon-r than air to boost capacitance without adding size, which is precisely the tool explored next.

The formula also explains, without any extra assumptions, why moving the plates closer together increases capacitance, since d sits in the denominator, and why increasing the overlapping area increases capacitance, since A sits in the numerator. Every practical decision in capacitor design, rolling foil tighter, choosing a thinner insulating film, or picking a material with higher permittivity, is really just an engineer pulling one of these three levers: A, d, or epsilon.
